extracted.intended_audience: teachers, students, parents, mathematicians, and general readers interested in mathematics education
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for presenting and teaching mathematics as a human-centered, exploratory endeavor that cultivates character and intellectual virtues rather than a set of procedures to be memorized. Emphasizes pedagogical attitudes, classroom practices, and the values mathematics can build.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as an exploratory quest
rubrics_metrics.description: Real math is a quest driven by curiosity and wonder; it requires creativity, aesthetic sensibilities, a penchant for mystery, and courage in the face of the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present math as exploratory adventure rather than rote procedure. Encourage playing with ideas, asking questions, collaborating, looking for patterns, breaking paradigms, recognizing beauty, and making convincing arguments (conjecture → theorem). Anti-pattern: treating math as memorizing terminology or following centuries-old procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing math to methods and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Math cannot be reduced to methods and applications (or to workbooks and drills); doing so misrepresents the heart of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate mathematics' value solely with utility. Instead communicate broader purposes and values that entice learners to engage. Example anti-pattern: presenting math primarily as a collection of techniques for practical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate specific human virtues through math
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics builds character and is organized around virtues such as 'imagination,' 'persistence,' 'hopefulness,' 'confidence in struggle,' 'disposition toward beauty,' 'inventiveness,' 'joyfulness,' and 'love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities and messaging that intentionally develop these virtues. Use examples, stories, and reflection to connect mathematical practice to personal growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start real mathematical activity early through play
rubrics_metrics.description: Kids can start to do real math as soon as they can play with puzzles, draw pictures, and reason logically—before formal skills like multiplication or solving for x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include puzzles, visual tasks, and exploratory play in early grades. Examples given: cutting brownies, comparing rectangles, Sudoku variations, counting ants on a log, hemisphere/points problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate lessons by the questions students ask
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique the effectiveness of your lesson, not by what answers students give, but by what questions they ask (quotation from Fawn Nguyen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize fostering curiosity and question-asking as indicators of learning. Use student questions to assess depth and engagement rather than solely correct answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value mistakes and struggle as productive
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the value of mistakes and the importance of struggle: 'even wrong ideas soften the soil in which good ideas can grow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage risk-taking, treat incorrect ideas as learning opportunities, and normalize productive struggle. Anti-pattern: penalizing early-stage wrong ideas or presenting struggle as failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate background with ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Background is not the same as ability; a learner's background should not be taken as limiting their potential in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt inclusive practices, avoid assumptions about learners' capacities based on background, and provide welcoming entry points to mathematical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the freedoms of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'freedoms of mathematics' include the freedom to solve problems, to explore new directions, to open one's imagination, and to land in a welcoming community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster multiple approaches, exploratory projects, imaginative tasks, and classroom/community norms that invite participation. Anti-pattern: narrow, single-method instruction that restricts intellectual freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers' responsibility to welcome others
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have experienced mathematical freedoms have a responsibility to welcome others to those freedoms; teachers are in a special position to foster and have an obligation to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make deliberate outreach, mentorship, and classroom practices that create welcoming spaces for newcomers; consider the social and ethical dimensions of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-centered exposition and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-centered exposition (personal details, stories) helps make mathematics accessible and relatable—for example Su uses personal history and correspondence to humanize math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate anecdotes, personal narratives, and human contexts to connect abstract ideas to learners' experiences. Anti-pattern: purely impersonal, heavily symbolic presentation with no human context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include intriguing puzzles and concrete examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use engaging puzzles and concrete problems to demonstrate mathematical enchantment and to entice learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a variety of accessible yet thought-provoking problems (e.g., geometric comparisons, combinatorial puzzles, parity/placement problems) as hooks for deeper exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address students' question about usefulness by reframing value
rubrics_metrics.description: When students ask 'When am I ever going to use this?' they are often asking 'When am I ever going to value this?' — teaching should reveal values beyond mere utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe lessons to highlight intrinsic values (beauty, creativity, character-building) and diverse reasons to value mathematics, rather than defaulting to practical application arguments.
